title: Breaking work into functions
summary: Name a job, give it inputs and an output, and build big results from small functions. Delve gets its status line, made of your earlier pieces.

steps.title: A function is a named job
body: A **function** packages a piece of work under a name. It takes **parameters** (inputs) and **returns** a result (output). Calling it copies your arguments into the parameter boxes, runs the body, and hands back the return value.
C#          int Square(int x) { return x * x; }
Python      def square(x): return x * x
JavaScript  function square(x) { return x * x; }
Why bother? **Decomposition**: a big problem becomes several small ones, each with a name you can read, test and reuse. `Hypotenuse` below reads like the maths because the details live in `Square`.

code: int Add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
steps.explain: Inner calls happen first: `Add(2, 3)` is 5, doubled is 10. Then `Twice(2)` is 4, plus 3 is 7.

steps.title: Pure functions and side effects
body: A **pure** function only reads its parameters and returns a value. Same inputs, same output, every time, and nothing else in the world changes.
A function has a **side effect** if it does anything else: prints, writes a file, changes a variable outside itself, reads the clock.

Pure functions are easier to test (call it, check the answer) and to trust. Side effects are necessary (a program that prints nothing is useless) but keep them at the edges: compute with pure functions, then print the result in one place.

steps.prompt: Pure, or has a side effect?
items: `int Max(int a, int b) => a > b ? a : b;`
steps.explain: Reading the clock is a side effect too: call it next year and the answer changes.

steps.prompt: Parameters are copies. What does this print?
steps.explain: `Bump` changes its own copy `s` and throws it away. `Bumped` returns the new value, and the caller chooses to store it.

steps.prompt: Arrange the program so it prints `Total: 23`. The main code comes first; the helper function goes at the end.
lines: foreach (int i in items) s += i;

steps.title: Decompose the report
prompt: - `int Min(int[] a)` and `int Max(int[] a)`: smallest and largest values (arrays are never empty). Use loops.
- `string Range(int[] a)`: returns `"min..max (spread s)"` by **calling** `Min` and `Max`, where `s` is max minus min.
solution: foreach (int x in a) if (x < m) m = x;
foreach (int x in a) if (x > m) m = x;

forbid.message: Min and Max use loops, not LINQ

hints: `Min` and `Max` are best-so-far loops that start from `a[0]`.
In `Range`, call them once each and store the answers in boxes before building the string.

steps.title: Lining text up
body: A status line is easier to read when every part starts in the same column, turn after turn. `PadRight(width)` adds spaces to the end of a string until it is `width` characters long (a longer string is left alone); `PadLeft` adds them at the start. `new string('#', 4)` is `"####"`.
Building the line from small functions means each part can be tested on its own, and fixed in one place.

code: string bar = "[" + new string('#', 3) + new string('-', 2) + "]";

steps.title: The status line
prompt: Delve prints a status line under the map. Build it from small functions:

**`static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)`**: a bar of `width` characters inside brackets: `value * width / max` of them `'#'` (integer division), the rest `'-'`. `Bar(14, 20, 10)` is `"[#######---]"`, `Bar(0, 20, 10)` is `"[----------]"`.
**`static string Hud(int hp, int maxHp, int copper, int xp, int floor)`** joins four parts:
Do not redo old work: **call your own `Level(xp)`** (Whole numbers and fractions) and **`Coins(copper)`** (the State and values boss). The checks supply the reference versions of both.
starter: static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)
static string Hud(int hp, int maxHp, int copper, int xp, int floor)
solution: static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)
return "[" + new string('#', filled) + new string('-', width - filled) + "]";
static string Hud(int hp, int maxHp, int copper, int xp, int floor)
template: // src/Damage.cs, as the reference solution wrote it
static int Damage(int attack, int armour)
// src/Shop.cs, as the reference solution wrote it
static int ToCopper(int gold, int silver, int copper)
static string Change(int paid, int price)

require.message: Lines the parts up with PadRight

forbid.message: Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)
Uses the Level and Coins you already wrote, not new copies

hints: Bar: `int filled = value * width / max;` then two `new string(...)` calls between the brackets.
Hud: build each part in its own box, pad it, then add them up: `string health = $"HP {Bar(hp, maxHp, 10)} {hp}/{maxHp}".PadRight(24);`

build.title: Status line
build.unlocks: Delve shows a health bar, your level and your purse under the map.
